questions.question_stem: A learner says, "My bitcoin is inside my wallet app, so losing the app deletes the coins." Which correction is best?
questions.correct_answer: The coins are represented on-chain as UTXOs; the wallet manages keys, addresses, policies, and signatures that authorize spending them.
incorrect_answers: The coins are cached locally by the wallet app; the blockchain only records backup hints, labels, and recovery data for the app.
The coins are tracked on-chain as account balances; the wallet signs balance updates that nodes apply to the user's account.
The coins are stored under one permanent receiving address; the wallet keeps the password that unlocks the address for spending.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames a wallet as a local key and policy manager, not as a coin container. Spendable value remains on-chain as UTXOs controlled by the relevant spending conditions.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/bitcoin_02-BF-transactions_and_mining-slides-only.qmd: What Are Wallets? / Wallets As Spending Authority

questions.question_stem: Why can one seed phrase often recover many receiving addresses in a Bitcoin wallet?
questions.correct_answer: The wallet can deterministically derive many private keys, public keys, and addresses from the seed phrase.
incorrect_answers: The seed phrase lists every receiving address, so the wallet reloads addresses directly from the words.
The wallet can ask full nodes to restore a master account balance that was registered to the seed phrase.
The seed phrase stores copies of wallet UTXOs, so recovery rebroadcasts those outputs to the network.
questions.explanation: A deterministic wallet can regenerate a family of keys and addresses from one backup root. The seed phrase restores spending authority; it does not recreate coins outside the blockchain.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/bitcoin_02-BF-transactions_and_mining-slides-only.qmd: Wallets, Addresses, and Keys / Where Addresses Come From

questions.question_stem: Alice spends two UTXOs worth 0.60 BTC and 0.70 BTC to pay Bob 1.00 BTC, creates a 0.29 BTC change output, and has no other outputs. What fee does the transaction pay?
questions.correct_answer: 0.01 BTC, because fees are total input value minus total output value.
incorrect_answers: 0.29 BTC, because sender change is counted as revenue for miners.
0.30 BTC, because only Bob's output is subtracted from the inputs.
0.00 BTC, because creating a change output means no fee is left.
questions.explanation: The transaction consumes 1.30 BTC of inputs and creates 1.29 BTC of outputs. The missing 0.01 BTC is the implicit transaction fee.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/bitcoin_02-BF-transactions_and_mining-slides-only.qmd: Example Transaction / Change Addresses and Fees

questions.question_stem: A node receives a transaction whose input references a UTXO that was already spent in an earlier accepted block. Why is the new transaction invalid under the UTXO model?
questions.correct_answer: A transaction input must consume a currently unspent output; once that output has been spent, it cannot be used again.
incorrect_answers: A transaction input is valid if the wallet controls enough total UTXO value, even when this exact output was already used.
A spent output can be reused if the new transaction pays a higher fee than the transaction that spent it in an earlier block.
An input only needs a valid signature for the referenced output; nodes do not check whether the output remains unspent.
questions.explanation: The UTXO model simplifies validation by making each input point to a discrete previous output. Double-spend checks reduce to whether that referenced output is still unspent and unlocked correctly.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/bitcoin_02-BF-transactions_and_mining-slides-only.qmd: UTXO Visualized / Why the UTXO Model?

questions.question_stem: A valid signed transaction has propagated to several nodes and is visible in their mempools. What is still missing before it has one confirmation?
questions.correct_answer: A miner must include it in a valid block that full nodes accept as part of the chain.
incorrect_answers: It must appear in every reachable node's mempool before any miner may include it in a block.
The receiving wallet must sign it before miners can place the payment in a valid block.
A full node must turn the mempool entry into a local balance update before it can be mined.
questions.explanation: Mempool presence means a transaction is an unconfirmed candidate for block inclusion. One confirmation begins only after the transaction is mined into an accepted block.

questions.question_stem: During a crowded mempool period, two valid transactions are waiting for inclusion. Why would miners usually prefer the one with the higher fee rate?
questions.correct_answer: Miners have limited block space and collect fees from included transactions, so higher-fee transactions are economically more attractive.
incorrect_answers: Higher fee rate proves the transaction transfers a larger bitcoin amount, so miners prioritize it over smaller payments with lower values.
Higher fee rate lowers the proof-of-work target for that block, making the candidate block easier for a miner to find under network congestion.
Higher fee rate lets the transaction skip ordinary full-node validation after it is included in a block, reducing the miner's orphan risk after relay.
questions.explanation: The lesson connects fee choice to confirmation speed. Miners choose among mempool transactions under block constraints and are incentivized by fees, but fee payment does not replace validation.

questions.question_stem: A transaction inside a block is changed after the miner found a valid proof-of-work. What would this do to the block's commitment structure?
questions.correct_answer: It would change the Merkle root, which changes the block header hash and breaks the previously found proof-of-work.
incorrect_answers: It would change only the local wallet record for nodes, leaving the Merkle root and block header hash unchanged.
It would require recomputing the transaction signatures, but the old proof-of-work would still match the same header.
It would change the previous block hash pointer while leaving the current block transaction commitment intact.
questions.explanation: The Merkle root commits the header to the block's transaction list. Altering a transaction changes that commitment and therefore the header hash that proof-of-work was found over.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/bitcoin_02-BF-transactions_and_mining-slides-only.qmd: The Data Structure of a Block / Transactions in a Block

questions.question_stem: A miner broadcasts a block with a valid-looking proof-of-work, but one transaction spends an already-spent output. What should full nodes do?
questions.correct_answer: Reject the block, because miners propose blocks but full nodes independently validate transaction validity and unspent inputs.
incorrect_answers: Accept it temporarily, because valid proof-of-work lets later confirmations repair an invalid transaction after peers build on top.
Forward it for miner replacement, because mining pools decide whether referenced outputs are still unspent before full nodes accept it.
Accept the valid transactions in the block and ignore only the double-spending transaction inside it during validation.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes miner proposal from full-node acceptance. Valid proof-of-work is necessary but not sufficient; peers also validate the transactions and chain extension rules.

questions.question_stem: What are miners trying to accomplish when they vary the nonce and related block fields during proof-of-work?
questions.correct_answer: Find a block header hash below the current difficulty target.
incorrect_answers: Choose the transaction set that pays the highest total fees.
Find a previous block hash that points to the current chain tip.
Make the coinbase output match the block subsidy and fees.
questions.explanation: Mining is a target-based search over candidate block headers. Miners repeatedly hash modified headers until one hash satisfies the network difficulty target.

questions.question_stem: A merchant accepts a zero-confirmation payment for a high-value item because the transaction is visible in a mempool. Which risk assessment is most accurate?
questions.correct_answer: The payment has not yet gained probabilistic settlement security; inclusion and additional confirmations reduce reversal risk.
incorrect_answers: It has the same settlement security as several confirmations because mempool relay shows nodes accepted it into their candidate ledgers.
Its main remaining risk is only slow wallet display; a relayed transaction cannot conflict with another spend of the same UTXO.
It becomes final once enough peers store it in their mempools, even before any block includes it in the chain history.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin finality is probabilistic. A transaction becomes more secure after block inclusion and as additional blocks build on top, while zero-confirmation payments carry greater double-spend or non-inclusion risk.

questions.question_stem: In Bitcoin's transaction model, why does a normal input need both a previous transaction identifier and an output index?
questions.correct_answer: Together they form an outpoint that identifies the exact previous output being spent.
incorrect_answers: Together, they identify the sender's account and the sequence number of the next withdrawal.
Together, they identify a block height and the transaction's confirmation count.
Together, they identify the input script and a private key for unlocking value.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes that an input points to a specific prior output, not to a user account. The transaction identifier plus output index lets nodes locate the exact UTXO and its spending conditions.

questions.question_stem: A transaction creates many tiny outputs that are technically possible under consensus rules, but most nodes refuse to relay it as dust. What distinction does this illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Consensus validity and relay or mining policy are not identical; policy can discourage outputs that burden the UTXO set.
incorrect_answers: Consensus rules require nodes to relay every valid transaction they see, even when outputs are uneconomical for wallets.
Relay policy can make a transaction valid even when consensus rules would reject one of its spends in a block at validation time.
Dust policy mainly protects miners from large signatures, not the growing UTXO database maintained by full nodes.
questions.explanation: The reading uses dust and standardness policy to show that not every technically valid transaction pattern is relayed or mined by default. Tiny UTXOs impose ongoing costs on full-node operators.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/mastering_bitcoin_ch06.adoc: Consensus Rules Versus Policy / Uneconomical outputs and disallowed dust

questions.question_stem: A contract protocol builds a child transaction that depends on a parent's transaction ID before the parent confirms. Why was transaction malleability dangerous for this pattern?
questions.correct_answer: If authorization data could be changed in a way that changed the parent's txid, the child transaction's reference could break even though the spend was otherwise valid.
incorrect_answers: If witness data changed, it would reveal the parent's private key to the child spender before either transaction confirmed, letting the child spend other outputs from the same wallet.
If the parent changed, the child would spend the whole parent transaction instead of one specific output index, consuming every output together from that parent.
If the parent was unconfirmed, nodes would require each child transaction to confirm first, creating a circular confirmation rule for dependent contract spends.
questions.explanation: The reading connects malleability to dependent and presigned transactions. Segwit reduces this problem by separating witness data from the txid calculation, improving txid stability for contract protocols.
